ch12.anchor: Sun Qi's Records of the Northern Ward
ch12.note: Records of the Northern Ward (Beili zhi) is a late-Tang account by Sun Qi of the Ping’kang ward, the licensed courtesans’ quarter in the north of the capital, Chang’an. From it beili, “the northern ward,” passed into literary Chinese as a standing byword for the brothel district — the sense the newspaper report plays on here.
Ni Zan (1301–1374), one of the Four Masters of the Yuan, celebrated for spare, tranquil ink landscapes of rock, water and a few bare trees. The source names him by his sobriquet Ni Yu.

ch12.anchor: the lewd music of Zheng and Wei
ch12.note: In the Confucian classics the songs of the ancient states of Zheng and Wei were the byword for licentious, morally loosening music, set against the upright music of the sages; “the sounds of Zheng” is a standard figure for corrupting art. Qian Huafo uses it to say the Little Garden had sunk wholly into vice.

The “Noulens” couple — Hilaire Noulens (a cover name of Yakov Rudnik) and his wife — were Comintern liaison agents in Shanghai. Their arrest in June 1931 laid bare much of the Comintern’s Far Eastern network; an international campaign to save them, joined by Song Qingling and Smedley, failed. Their case threads through this book’s intelligence story.

ch12.anchor: Yang Xingfo and others got wind
ch12.note: Yang Xingfo (Yang Quan, 1893–1933), a US-trained scholar and administrator, secretary-general of the Academia Sinica and executive secretary of the Civil Rights League. Blue Shirt gunmen assassinated him in Shanghai on June 18, 1933, on the steps of the Academia Sinica — the killing recounted later in this chapter.

ch12.anchor: through the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
ch12.note: The China League for the Protection of Civil Rights (Zhongguo minquan baozhang tongmeng), a civil-liberties body founded in Shanghai in December 1932 under Song Qingling, with Cai Yuanpei, Lu Xun and Yang Xingfo. It campaigned for the release of political prisoners; after Yang Xingfo’s assassination in June 1933 it effectively ceased to exist.

Agnes Smedley (1892–1950), American radical journalist and author of the autobiographical novel Daughter of Earth. A committed supporter of the Chinese Communists, she reported from China through the 1930s. Her recollections here are a partisan witness’s; the author sets them against the contemporary newspaper record below and finds them wrong on several points.

ch12.anchor: the young American reporter Harold Isaacs
ch12.note: Harold Isaacs (1910–1986), American journalist then in Shanghai, where he edited the left-wing China Forum; later the author of The Tragedy of the Chinese Revolution (1938), a classic account written from a dissident-left standpoint.

ch12.anchor: Lin Yutang, Lu Xun and others were on the executive
ch12.note: Lin Yutang (1895–1976), essayist and editor, at this time an officer of the Civil Rights League; a few years later, with My Country and My People (1935), he became the best-known interpreter of China to English-speaking readers.

ch12.anchor: Hu Shi, too, in his Independent Critic
ch12.note: Hu Shi (1891–1962), the foremost liberal intellectual of Republican China and a champion of writing in the vernacular; his weekly the Independent Critic (Duli pinglun) ran from 1932. Printing the mayor’s flat denial places him here on the government’s side of the case — a stance the League’s people held against him.

The Blue Shirts Society (Lanyishe), a secret ultranationalist paramilitary formed within the Kuomintang in 1932 on an avowedly fascist model, used for surveillance, intimidation and political murder. Its gunmen carried out Yang Xingfo’s assassination.
L’Impartial (Da Gong Bao), a leading independent Chinese daily founded in Tianjin in 1902; the French title was the paper’s own.

ch12.anchor: a well-known poet of the Lakeside school
ch12.note: The Lakeside Poetry Society (Hupan), founded at Hangzhou’s West Lake in 1922 by Ying Xiuren, Wang Jingzhi and others, known for fresh, direct love-lyrics. Ying Xiuren was one of its founders.

The Mukden, or September 18, Incident of 1931: the Japanese Kwantung Army’s staged pretext for seizing Manchuria. It set off the scattered anti-Japanese volunteer resistance in the Northeast mentioned here.

Jiang Boyue is Jiang Wei (202–264), the last great general of Shu Han. After his state fell he feigned surrender to the conquering Wei in a bid to restore it from within; the plot was found out and he was killed. Meng Huating means their own feigned surrender has come to the same ruin.
